description: We are an interdisciplinary team combining data analysis, engineering, and a passion for space exploration. Through MOON BASE FIRE READINESS, we translate raw scientific data from NASA orbital experiments into concrete design guidelines and safety procedures to protect future crewed lunar and Martian missions from fire hazards.
summary:
Moon Base Fire Readiness is a dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion record into an answer to one question: what do we actually know about fire in the atmospheres planned for exploration, such as the Artemis Moon base at 30% oxygen and 10.2 psi?

We curated 24 combustion investigations and 243 individual test runs from the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. Every field carries its source and locator, and every field extracted from text carries a verbatim quote and was checked by a team member against its source. The app ranks investigations by relevance to a chosen habitat, maps which oxygen and pressure conditions have been tested, and estimates flammability with a hybrid method: nearest test runs where they exist, and an adiabatic flame temperature margin calibrated on FLEX droplet limits where they do not. Outside the tested envelope the answer is "no evidence", with a physics estimate labelled as such.

An AI-generated report summarizes the evidence for each habitat and may cite only investigations in the curated data. The main finding: no solid material in the PSI microgravity data was tested at Moon base conditions, and experiments such as FM2 and LUCI are needed to close that gap.
details:
What it does
- Habitat Lens: pick an atmosphere (Earth, ISS, Orion, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars habitat scenario, spacesuit, and the NASA exploration atmospheres at 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 and 8.2 psia / 34% O2) and see which PSI investigations are relevant and why, with every score explained.
- Gap map: every tested condition plotted against the habitat atmospheres. Solid-material tests stop at about 22% O2 and 1 atm; the Moon base sits outside all of them.
- Predictor with confidence: distance-weighted nearest-neighbour vote over test runs in a scaled condition space (adiabatic flame temperature, log pressure, flow), with an envelope check on each dimension before any neighbour search. When the target is outside the data, it reports "no evidence" plus a physics-only margin labelled as an estimate. Confidence is evidence coverage, not a probability of fire.
- Cited report: a language model writes a summary per habitat from the curated data only. A validator strips any citation that is not in the data and rejects texts that make claims the data do not support, for example that 0 g and 1 g tests bound lunar gravity or that fire-resistant materials are safe. If the model is unavailable or the text is rejected, a cached report is served.
- Investigation pages: every field with its source, quote and verification state, the publication list, and which ground studies reused each flight experiment's data.
- Smoke detection simulator (illustrative model, not a validated one): the same fire, vents and detectors in a generic module run side by side in 0 g and 1 g, showing why detector placement depends on gravity and air flow. It sits next to the findings of the NASA smoke experiments SAME, SAME-R and DAFT, including the SAME / SAME-R disagreement on smoke particle size.

Physics
We computed adiabatic flame temperatures with Cantera and NASA Glenn thermodynamic data. The published FLEX limiting oxygen indices in nitrogen and with CO2 dilution give the same limiting flame temperature per fuel (1674/1657 K for methanol, 1910/1908 K for n-heptane), which is why we use flame temperature as the physics axis. It fails for helium, and we say so. Microgravity is not partial gravity: NASA's FM2 team reports that lunar gravity may be close to the most flammable condition, so 0 g and 1 g data do not bound the Moon.

Honest evaluation
Leave-one-out on 235 runs (fire-resistant materials excluded): droplets reproduce the published limits, which is a consistency check, not a forecast. For solids the predictor does no better than "always sustained", because 131 of 134 ordinary solid runs in PSI are sustained. We report this openly; the value of the tool is showing where evidence exists and where it does not.

Why it matters
Exploration habitats will run at higher oxygen and lower pressure than the ISS. Decisions about materials and fire response there should rest on evidence, and this tool shows exactly how much evidence there is.

Tools
Next.js, React, TypeScript, zod, d3-scale, Vitest; a Web Worker and canvas for the smoke simulator; Python with Cantera 3.2 for the offline flame temperature calculation; deployed on Vercel. The report uses the openai/gpt-oss-120b model served by Groq. Open source under Apache 2.0.

Use of AI
A language model extracted part of the curated fields (summaries, key findings, fuel, variables, measurements) from PSI records and publication abstracts. Each such field keeps a verbatim quote and was checked by a team member against its source, and a script checks every PSI quote word for word. AI assistants also helped find NASA photos and sources, write code (Claude Code), draft and edit text, design the interface and build the presentation. The logo was generated with an AI image generator and carries an "AI-generated" watermark. Every number in the app comes from NASA sources, never from a model's memory.
